title: Particle physics
subtitle: A bounded introductory problem-solving path

lessons.title: Events are evidence not little pictures
lessons.idea: Detectors record interactions from which particle properties are inferred.
body: A particle in quantum field theory is an excitation associated with a field. A detector does not photograph a tiny classical ball; it records deposited energy, tracks, timing or other interactions.
An event is a collection of measurements from one collision or decay. A particle interpretation must predict patterns across many such events, including efficiencies and backgrounds.

body: Particle tables often use GeV for energy, GeV/c for momentum and GeV/c² for mass. A gigaelectronvolt is one billion electronvolts.
Setting c=1 is a unit convention that simplifies equations. Restore the factors when converting to SI units or comparing different physical quantities.

lessons.title: Antiparticles reverse some labels
lessons.idea: An antiparticle has the same mass as its partner but opposite additive charges.
body: A positron is the electron antiparticle: its electric charge is positive rather than negative. Antimatter is not negative mass or matter moving with negative energy in a detector.
Neutral particles still need careful labels. Some neutral particles are their own antiparticles; others have distinct antiparticles because of other quantum numbers.

apply.text: Why must a proposed annihilation conserve momentum too?
apply.answer: Opposite charges can cancel in total, but charge conservation is only one constraint. The complete outgoing state must also match total energy and momentum.

lessons.title: A resonance is short lived
lessons.idea: Unstable particles can appear as peaks in reconstructed invariant-mass distributions.
body: A short-lived state may decay before leaving a visible track. Its existence can be inferred from a repeated pattern in its decay products.
The intrinsic resonance width relates to lifetime, but the observed peak also includes detector resolution and production dynamics. A bump alone is not automatically a new particle.

lessons.title: Organize quarks and leptons
lessons.idea: The matter fields fall into quark and lepton families with different interaction charges.
body: Quarks carry color charge and participate in the strong interaction. Leptons do not carry color; charged leptons also interact electromagnetically, and neutrinos participate in weak interactions.
The three generations repeat charge patterns with different masses. Generation is not a stage through which one particle grows as it gets older.

The first generation contains up and down quarks, the electron and electron neutrino. The second contains charm and strange quarks, the muon and muon neutrino. The third contains top and bottom quarks, the tau and tau neutrino. Each charged-lepton name labels its associated neutrino flavor; flavor states are not the same as neutrino mass states.
lessons.terms: e: positive elementary electric charge (C). The fractional values describe quark charges; isolated quarks are not observed as free asymptotic particles.

lessons.title: Interactions follow a gauge framework
lessons.idea: Gauge symmetry organizes the interactions rather than describing a literal exchange of tiny ropes.
body: The Standard Model uses electromagnetic, weak and strong gauge structures. Their associated force fields and matter couplings are constrained by this mathematical framework.
Gauge freedom includes different descriptions of the same physical situation. Observable predictions must not depend on a mere choice of description.
lessons.equation: Same physical state + changed gauge description → same observables
lessons.terms: gauge description, observables: redundant mathematical description and measurable quantities (not numerical units). An observable is a quantity accessible through a measurement prediction.

lessons.title: Hadrons are composite
lessons.idea: A proton is a strong-interaction bound system rather than an elementary particle.
body: Hadrons contain quark and gluon degrees of freedom. A valence-quark label captures important conserved quantum numbers, but not every fluctuating constituent in the full quantum state.
Baryons include three-valence-quark patterns; ordinary mesons use quark-antiquark patterns. More complicated hadronic structures also exist.

lessons.title: Separate success from open questions
lessons.idea: A successful theory can have clearly identified limits.
body: The Standard Model describes an enormous range of measured particle processes, but it is not a complete theory of every physical phenomenon.

Gravity, the identity of dark matter, the origin of observed neutrino masses and the cosmic matter-antimatter imbalance remain questions requiring additional explanation or extensions. A gap is not proof of one favored speculative answer.

lessons.idea: A transformation changes a description; an invariant stays the same under that change.
body: Rotate your coordinate axes and vector components change, but the physical length does not. Lorentz transformations similarly change energy and momentum components while preserving invariant mass.
Always name the transformation. A quantity can be invariant under rotations without being unchanged under every possible physical operation.

lessons.title: Continuous symmetry links to conservation
lessons.idea: A continuous symmetry of the dynamics can imply a conserved quantity.
body: If the laws do not change when the time origin shifts, energy conservation follows under the assumptions of Noether reasoning. Spatial-translation symmetry similarly connects to momentum.
This concerns symmetry of the full dynamics, not merely a picture that looks symmetric. External time-dependent driving can transfer energy into a subsystem.

lessons.idea: Reversing space and replacing particles by antiparticles are different operations.
body: Parity reverses spatial coordinates, like comparing a process with its inverted spatial arrangement. Charge conjugation swaps particle labels for antiparticle labels.
The weak interaction does not preserve parity, and some processes violate combined CP symmetry. A symmetry must be tested for the interaction, not assumed from an appealing mirror analogy.

lessons.title: Internal labels are not directions in the room
lessons.idea: Internal quantum numbers describe how states transform in an abstract state space.
body: Spin rotations relate to physical space, but other labels such as flavor or color belong to internal degrees of freedom. Calling color red is a mathematical label, not a visible pigment.
A representation tells how a symmetry transformation acts on a set of state components. It supplies a rule for changing the mathematical coordinates while preserving the theory structure.

The worked swap is an active internal operator: it changes the state while the chosen basis stays fixed. A passive basis change instead relabels the coordinates of the same state. Neither operation is necessarily a rotation of the detector in physical space; keep the two meanings separate.
lessons.equation: Transformed state components = transformation matrix × original components
lessons.terms: transformation matrix, components: linear map and state coordinates (no unit for normalized internal amplitudes). Matrix multiplication combines components according to a specified symmetry representation.

lessons.idea: Energy and all three momentum components must balance in a decay.
body: Four-momentum packages energy and spatial momentum into one relativistic object. Conservation applies component by component in any inertial frame.
In a parent rest frame, outgoing momenta must sum to zero. Their individual energies remain positive; opposite momenta do not cancel energy.

lessons.title: Two-body decay fixes rest-frame energies
lessons.idea: Two-body kinematics strongly constrains energy sharing in the parent rest frame.
body: With only two products, momentum conservation gives equal opposite momentum magnitudes. Equal momentum does not imply equal energy if product masses differ.
For two massless products, both energies are half the parent rest energy. This simple special case makes a useful starting point before the general massive formula.

For general daughter masses, let M be parent mass and m1,m2 the daughter masses, all in GeV/c². In the parent rest frame E1=(M²+m1²−m2²)c²/(2M), E2=Mc²−E1 and p c=√[E1²−(m1c²)²]. Here E1,E2 are total energies in GeV, p is the common momentum magnitude in GeV/c, c is vacuum light speed, and √ means the nonnegative square root. The parent must satisfy M≥m1+m2; at equality there is no relative momentum. These equations come from conserving total energy and equal opposite momentum, together with each daughter energy-momentum relation.

For a fresh unequal-mass example, use rest energies Mc²=5 GeV, m1c²=3 GeV and m2c²=0. Then E1=(25+9−0)/(2×5)=3.4 GeV, E2=5−3.4=1.6 GeV and pc=√(3.4²−3²)=1.6 GeV. The daughters have different total energies but equal opposite momenta of magnitude 1.6 GeV/c.

The parent is at rest and the complete final state contains exactly two products; the original equal-energy example uses two massless products. lessons.title: A small coupling supports an expansion

For low-energy electromagnetic interactions, the fine-structure constant α (alpha) is approximately 1/137. It is a dimensionless measure of electromagnetic coupling strength. The effective α changes with probing scale, so 1/137 is not a universal high-energy value. Small α motivates many electromagnetic expansions, subject to the additional limitations just described.

lessons.title: Strong coupling depends on scale
lessons.idea: Short-distance weak coupling and long-distance confinement describe different regimes.
body: At sufficiently high momentum transfer, quark and gluon interactions can often be treated with a smaller effective strong coupling. This is asymptotic freedom.

At long distances, isolated colored particles are not observed as free final states. Confinement and hadron formation require nonperturbative reasoning, not a simple extrapolation of the high-energy expansion.

body: Writing a mass parameter in an equation is not always compatible with the gauge symmetries assigned to the fields. The Standard Model distinguishes different field transformation properties.

lessons.title: The Higgs field and boson differ
lessons.idea: The field background and a particle excitation of that field are not identical concepts.
body: A field can have a nonzero vacuum value even when no real Higgs boson is being detected. The Higgs boson is an excitation around that vacuum configuration.

Couplings to the Higgs field give charged elementary fermions and W/Z bosons their mass terms in the Standard Model. The minimal original Standard Model does not supply the observed neutrino masses; their origin requires an extension and remains unresolved. The measured Higgs boson tests the mechanism but does not by itself explain the numerical pattern of every coupling.

lessons.title: Missing momentum is an imbalance
lessons.idea: Missing transverse momentum summarizes an imbalance in reconstructed visible momentum.
body: A calorimeter measures energy deposited when particles create cascades, or showers, of secondary interactions in material. A calibrated electrical or light signal estimates the deposited energy. Leakage outside the instrument, incomplete response and finite resolution can make that estimate differ from the original particle energy. Energy is a scalar; momentum has direction. Combining calibrated energy measurements with track directions helps reconstruct visible objects before calculating an imbalance.

Add the measured visible transverse momentum vectors, then reverse that sum. The result estimates unobserved transverse momentum if the initial transverse balance and detector response are understood.
Neutrinos can cause missing momentum, but so can mismeasurement, acceptance gaps and backgrounds. Missing energy is evidence to model, not a unique particle label.

lessons.title: Know where the bridge ends
lessons.idea: Introductory particle reasoning prepares questions that a full quantum field theory can answer.
body: You can now distinguish kinematics, rates, detector response and statistical evidence. These are complementary parts of a claim, not substitutes for one another.

Calculating amplitudes from a quantum field theory requires relativistic fields, symmetry representations, quantization, perturbation methods and renormalization. This course introduces their roles without pretending to derive the full machinery.

Bounded examples of open questions are the particle identity of dark matter, the mechanism generating neutrino masses and the origin of the cosmic matter–antimatter asymmetry. Evidence for an unexplained phenomenon is not evidence for every proposed explanation. Distinguish established observations, a model prediction and an unconfirmed candidate mechanism.

apply.answer: Strengthen special relativity, linear algebra, quantum amplitudes, classical fields and symmetry reasoning, then study a structured field-theory course with explicit calculations.
